chapter: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
title: No academic system yet for jazz study
summary: Hinton argues jazz lacks an organized curriculum, citing Japanese bands that play every style, and urges Ted Jr. to build one.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Well, Teddy, your dad mentioned that we talked about the commercialism of it, which is sterile, as he said, which is done just to get profits.
The whole picture will tell the tale.

Then American jazz, which is a creative art form, has not been pinpointed and has not been categorized or organized into the form of study yet. You might try it and I might try to present what we can, but we have no academic system of saying American Jazz History Number One, American Jazz Music -- 2-a, or something. It's young, the country is 200 years old, and even the system of teaching jazz in the universities is something new, and it's going to be people like you, Teddy, Jr. that's gonna have to organize this and set up a curriculum that says that you can't take Jazz History Number One unless you know about Budd Johnson, or you can't go into Jazz History No. 3, you can't play in this band unless you have played in a band like Louis Armstrong. And when your father goes to Japan and he plays with bands there, the people out there, the girls and singers like Billie Holiday, the Guy Lombardo bands in Japan, there are Duke Ellington bands in Japan, there are Count Basie bands -- these people are, in organizing their love for our jazz music, they have gone in all these categories, and we have some bypassing it, and it's gonna be people like you that's gonna have to help us do that. I mean, today is here, and someday we'll be gone.
